title: Talking about Dark Retreat, Part 2 with Andrew Holecek

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for metamodern mutants interested in meditation, awakening, non-dual Shaiva Tantra, deity yoga, jhanas, Spinoza, predictive processing, psychedelics, non-duality, consciousness hacking, and much, much more. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode I'm speaking with Andrew Holecek. Andrew Holecek is an interdisciplinary scholar, practitioner in Tibetan Buddhism and other non-dual wisdom traditions. He is a resident contemplative scholar at the Institute for Advanced Consciousness Studies and a research consultant for the Cognitive Neuroscience Program at Northwestern University. His work involves studies on dream yoga and the practice of dark retreat, and he is the author of nine books. In my recent program with Andrew, which was called Talking About Dark Retreat, we decided to continue the conversation at a later time because there was just so much interesting material there. Well, we ended up doing that, and this episode is part two of Talking About Dark Retreat. So, without further ado, I give you Talking About Dark Retreat, part two, with Andrew Holecek.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Andrew, welcome back once again to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Michael, so great once again to hang with you. So appreciate the time.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Thanks. And we're doing this rather quickly after the last one, because we did kind of promise to do a part two about the darkness material, which I'm super excited about. And, you know, something else, which is in the meantime, since part one has come out, I've noticed just a tremendous amount of interest in this topic, not only the podcast we did, but the topic in general, looking on, I don't know what to call it, but let's say meditation or Dharma Twitter and other places. This darkness stuff is, for some reason, really hitting a nerve, and I'm curious if you have any ideas why that might be, and if you're experiencing that, or am I just making it up?

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: No, you're definitely not making it up. It's one reason that I elected to come out of the closet, almost literally in this case, and riff on this stuff is because it's definitely getting out there. Interest is really growing, borderline exploding. And I think as more psychonauts, spelunkers of the mind, nyctophiliacs, lovers of the night and darkness like myself, taste this amazing medicine, you're going to see more and more of it because of all the extraordinary restorative aspects that we hinted at in our last conversation together. We can circle back to some of those things. And I reflected on this quite a bit. And my conjecture around this, and curious how this lands with you, is that there's something ineffably profound about darkness. I mentioned last time this notion of it's like a Rorschach practice where we project so many things onto this metaphysical mirror, but for some people repulsive because it represents this kind of death space, they're afraid of it. For other people, especially some Gen Xers, whoever, I don't even know what the new generation is called, it's kind of cool because it's got this goth quality and that's kind of magnetizing. But in my experience, and I've noticed this in some social situations, there's something elemental about darkness. There's some inarticulate, archetypal, primordial quality to this that is magnetizing because it represents origins, right? I mean, I can't recall if we talked about this last time, but allegedly, we don't know for sure, but allegedly prior to the big flash of the Big Bang, well, it had to flash out of something. Otherwise, it wouldn't be a flash. So we could conjecture that that came out of a primordial bedrock of darkness. In the book of Genesis, darkness precedes light. In many, many world mythologies, manifest reality arises out of darkness. We were conceived in darkness, more likely, spent nine months in it, and then came into the world. We're going to return to darkness. If you look at your mind, out of the background radiation of the elemental mind arises the light, the luminous display of thoughts, emotions and everything else that arises. So I think, Michael, it has to do with this kind of maybe even genetic level resonance with just what darkness represents. It represents depth and interiority and intimacy and all the things, by the way, that I think are sadly missing in this age. And I've been thinking a little bit more about this, we can go back to this later because it's a topic I just want to put it on the table, how darkness, this dark medicine, can serve as a magnificent potential remedy or counterbalancing measure to things like AI. So I'll pause because that's a different track, but I think it has to do something like that. There's something so ineffably deep, intimate, profound, archetypal about this that is magnetizing for people.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It does make sense. And we could go in a Jungian direction and say how our culture is strongly overbalanced in the mental, rational, conscious, light forces, the solar forces. And here is almost like not just a symbol or representation, but an actual experience, almost like physical experience of the primordial, the chaos, the darkness, the lunar, the feminine, all that right there. It's not a symbol. You're in it. The other thing that it reminds me of culturally, and this is maybe a counterpoint almost to what I was just saying, it's got the hardcore-ness that people like of like the Wim Hof thing and the ice baths and all that kind of like extreme sports sort of feel of some parts of the spiritual journey, right?

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: For sure, yeah. The non-negotiable, uncompromising nature of it is, it's like a challenge for people. It's like, you know, what can I do with this? But you suggested something here that's worth pinging around. I want to put an exclamation point on something you said. I think another reason people are interested in this practice is because there's an underlying intuition about loss of the feminine. And this warrants just a tiny riff. You know, in Buddhist tradition, light is masculine and darkness is feminine. And so when we step into the darkness, and this is actually my feeling when I go into it, I feel like I'm entering a primordial embrace of the feminine. And in fact, in Buddhist languaging, this was a massive experience for me. One particular retreat a number of years ago, I actually felt I was stepping into the dark and being held by the primordial mother. You know this term, Prajnaparamita, the mother of all Buddhas, the mother of the awakened mind.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: She's the mother of your awakened mind. And so it was one of the most beautiful feelings of meeting the deities. You know, they talk about you go into the dark to meet the gods and the deities. And this is another rich topic we can talk about, what does that really mean. Well, for me, meeting this and being embraced by the feminine and feeling the warm, loving embrace of the darkness was amazing. And also briefly, this gets really kind of sexy in the tantric truest sense, is this is a tantric meditation, dark retreat, and there are a number of unique characteristics of tantra, and one of these is that in tantra the female penetrates the male. And so when you're in the dark and darkness represents this feminine quality, and you open to it, you surrender to it, you allow the darkness to penetrate you, to saturate you, that's where all the restoration, the curative aspects take place. And then you're balancing this equation of otherwise runaway patriarchal energy, because have you noticed there's a little bit too much artificial light, literally. There's a little bit too much runaway patriarchy, literally. And so to me, I think another deep resonance here is, I say this with quite a bit of qualification, and everything's in quotation marks, but I think if one relates to dark medicine properly, I think it can be viewed as a kind of radical spiritual feminism, only in the sense that it balances this crazy runaway masculine energy with way too much light. So I think that's something definitely to put an exclamation point on that draws people.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, and of course, that would apply to both men and women. But our culture is so solar and so intense, we're so egoic and focused on mental achievement and the mind and all that, the mind in the sense of the cognition as being the primary function. And I would say that this feeling of even talking about dark retreat brings up this whole other thing, right? This whole letting go, and maybe even the challenge of encountering this primordial, what I like to call chaos, even though it's a different meaning of the word chaos, not confusion, but that sense of potential rather than actual or manifested. So what do you think about the other part of this, though, that almost counterbalances that feminine quality, which is the extreme sport quality of it, which I also sense in some of the interest.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Before I get to that, I just want to say one tiny important thing emphasizing what you just said, that whether we know it or not, we live in a solar-centric reality where there's a lot more solar deities than there are lunar deities. We live in a sight-centric culture, which is the most dominant sense faculty, the most dualistic sense faculty, where I can't remember the exact data, something like one third of brain processing power devoted to working with sense of sight, which is our most dualistic, superficial sense. We're a wake culture, where ironically it was the three main states of consciousness according to Hinduism and Buddhism, waking, dreaming, and deep dreamless sleep. Well...

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I was just reading some material last night from non-dual Shaiva Tantra: the waking state is the most contracted, the most out-of-touch state.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: That's right. The state with the least potential for psycho-spiritual evolution. And so as we have it completely bass-ackwards, as we actually fall asleep, and where are we falling? We're falling into darkness, right? We're falling awake if we maintain lucidity. So in other words, the waking state is a more real dimension. What did Thoreau say? In dreams, we are our truest life awake. And then if you maintain lucidity in the deep dreamless state, that's when you're the most awake. Ramana Maharshi famously said here, that which does not exist in deep dreamless sleep is not real. And so that's the other thing that's about this. So we have a sight-centric culture, a wake-centric culture, and a light-centric or photo-centric culture. And so because of this, all of these really in the service of the mother of all centricities, which is what? Egocentricity. And so this is another part of the balancing thing, that as we go into the dark, sight is taken away, light is taken away, wake in the normal sense is taken away. And when you get rid of these three centricities in the service of egocentricity, well, what does that do to the ego? It basically starts to deconstruct egoic structure, like we talked about last time. So this is another little, not little, I think major point about what darkness has to offer. And to come back to your question, for sure, going into the dark is a kind of a extreme sport as a way to test yourself against new metrics and all that. That I think is also one of the reasons that people are interested in it. We talked about this last time, some of the articles in sports magazines about people going into dark retreat is the next extreme meditation, extreme sport, that kind of thing. And like I said last time, boy, that is the absolute worst way to go into the dark, because then the only thing that's going to come out is just a stronger ego.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, this is the thing. It's the ego's way of trying to encounter the darkness, right? Instead of surrendering to it, it's to conquer it or whatever.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Exactly. Yeah. Good luck with that. It's a little bit like trying to conquer a high dose psychedelic. Get back to me on how well that works.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Exactly, especially if you think you're conquering it. Try a little bit more.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Yeah, that's exactly right. And that's the beauty of this practice. Just like with high dose psychedelics, just like, honestly, just like with death, you have to surrender. And that's what it invites at first, if you catch on to it. And then, just like death, non-negotiable, uncompromising, that is eventually what it demands. And that's why it is referred to as a forceful method of liberation, because it is non-negotiable and uncompromising. And so if you come in with this more feminine — this is interesting, a preliminary data, this is all anecdotal because we don't have it yet — but women tend to do better than men in the dark. They tend to resonate with it more. They tend to surrender to it more. They allow themselves to open up more, because as many women come out saying, I never felt so safe in my life as it was when I was in the dark. And paraphrasing a little bit, it's like nobody could see me, how I look didn't matter, appearances don't matter. The major aspect of dark retreat is all the things that wake centricity, sight centricity, light centricity focus on: appearance, it's gone. Appearances don't matter in the dark. And so think about what this does for people who deal with just body dysmorphias, and people who are aging, and people who have issues with physicality. You go into the dark and you realize these outer, superficial-most dimensions of my being, they don't matter in here, right? And so it's a wonderful way to balance the book, so to speak, to what really matters. At the end of the day — we use this phrase, right, at the end of the day, to denote what? What really counts? What matters at the end? What's important? What's really substantive? Well, what happens at the end of the day, Michael? It gets dark. And so darkness itself represents this quality of importance and essentiality, substance. And I think that's another reason people are magnetized. So I've kind of skidded around, but I do think it's important.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So interesting.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: So to me, those are some of the reasons, but I just want to see if there are any others that you're finding out there that I haven't noticed.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: For why people are magnetized?

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Yes, yes. Well, I think there's others. One is just so effing bizarre. I mean, it's just so different. And yeah, I can't recall everything I mentioned in our last conversation, but in the rare instances I do bring this up in public — I'm doing it more obviously, but I didn't used to — it's a conversation stopper because it's just so bloody different. And so I think that for people is magnetizing. It's outrageous. It puts people way out of their comfort zone. It takes them to the edge. It's mysterious. It's ineffable. And so you start to put all these ingredients together and you start to see like why there's this developing interest. And then especially when people are now coming out and posting on YouTube and Twitter and whatnot. I've listened to a number of these myself. It's really drawing a lot of traffic from people coming out with these kind of testimonials. But I'm curious, Michael, from your own side, for instance, when you first heard about it or where your thinking has gone along these lines, I mean, what are your thoughts here?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, besides the balancing out the solar, masculine, egoic quality of our culture, which is probably the most that has ever been in any culture, so it's a big deal, and also again the extreme sport quality, I think that it's also just — I'll say this in a positive way, but also in kind of, let's say, not so positive way — it's the next thing. Yeah, it's the new thing. So for a while there it was all about jhana, and then several different movements in the hardcore dharma field, and then for a while non-duality became the big buzzword, and then jhanas came back, and then now it's the dark. So in terms of the consumerist marketing world of dharmic teachings, it's the latest thing, right? And so that's kind of the not-so-positive way of saying it. But to touch upon that again in a little more gentle of a manner, for people who've done a lot of meditation or people who've done a lot, it's interesting, right? In my own case, again, my long meditation history, but part of it in there was working with Shinzen a lot for decades, Shinzen Young. And then what happened is I was using on my own a technique of his where you're really working very closely, in a close Vipassana way, with the arising of mental imagery. And that led to like some very significant breakthroughs for me, both in doing dream yoga stuff, which you and I talked about in the past, but also in understanding or directly seeing or clear seeing the construction of everything in awareness, all experience as a construction. And I was so naive in certain ways, I sort of thought I'd invented it. I didn't realize that's a whole way of working. So for me, this thing about the centrality of this deep, deep, deep clarity about the construction of the perceptual experience of being a person is obviously foundational, fundamental, and it seems to be the thing that darkness practice is going directly for.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: That is so spot on. Yeah, that is so spot on. Like, for instance, I mean, here's an analog. When people do arguably the ultimate kind of absorption practice, nirodha samapatti, which is like a post-jhana stage, sometimes called the ninth jhana, where consciousness itself is even turned off — well, one of the main reasons people do this is that when the mind comes back online, and this is highly analogous to what happens in the dark, is you're coming out of such an incredible dimension of cessation that when things start to come back into manifestation and you're approaching this from this point of complete cessation, you start to see things you've never seen before. For instance, like the 12 links of dependent origination, you know, the intellectual content of enlightenment, which arguably what the Buddha discovered that composed his awakening. This was made available to him and others who attain these levels of deep cessation, because the mind slows down and stops to such extent that when it comes back into gear, you start to see how the movie is stitched back together. You start to see how everything is superglued back together. And this is an amazing aspect of dark medicine as well. This is the reconstruction part. Because you go in — I mentioned this before, it really is like entering the death space. It's the main reason I continue to do it in the context of bardo yoga. But what I discovered very delightfully is that, yes, it's not merely just entering the painful bardo of dying, which is the first of the three death bardos, where one is fundamentally forced to let go. That's, by the way, what makes it painful, is the letting go. But then when you come out, you're stepping into the karmic bardo of becoming. And this is why it's the penultimate bardo practice, because when you step out of the dark, you start to see how the habit patterns kick back in. And habit is just a Western translation for karma. And so you literally see, in the most intimate, profound ways — it's to me one of the absolute most fascinating parts of the dark retreat is what happens when I come out. It's just breathtaking to see how everything comes back online, how I see the engine starting and how my perceptual world is stitched back together. Because literally, it's not just epistemological levels of deconstruction, but it's perceptual levels of deconstruction that take place in the dark. And so I come out, I literally don't see the world the same way. It takes me a while to stitch my world back together. It's not always particularly comfortable. It's actually a little bit like — I don't do LSD anymore for just this reason, because I do not enjoy the process of coming back into form, but it's somewhat analogous to that, but more enjoyable in the sense that I can titrate it and I can control it more. But I throw that into the works. And there was one thing you said, again, I want to just come back. It's the next new thing. Of course, it's not a new thing. It's been around for thousands of years. It's an old thing that's just being recycled. And the last thing I wanted to say, just parenthetically, to why people go in, I'm hearing this a lot these days, is darkness also represents deep restoration, deep rest. The capacity to go in there and just really recover on a purely biophysical level. That should not be dismissed, by the way. Something about going in there and sleeping for 14, 16 hours a day for the first couple of days, there's nothing wrong with that at all. Because that's another part of the equation that gets balanced when you're in the dark. You don't realize how sleep deprived you are. You don't realize how your body is craving this level of deep restoration. And so this is another thing that's also from a purely physiological, biological level is, I think, another very compelling reason why people are magnetized to this. But I just wanted to tuck that in as a parenthetical interjection.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, there's so many threads to pull out there. But I do want to say that makes perfect sense, the deep restoration point. But of course, it's a little bit at odds with the challenging, uncomfortable, outrageous, difficult nature of dark retreat. And I assume that has to do with how long you're in there.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Exactly. Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So I'm, of course, very intrigued by dark retreat's analogous function, where you start with nirodha samapatti or other practice like that, where it gives you the opportunity to watch the brain start to reconstruct its model of the world, right? And my question there might be either super easy to answer or maybe quite difficult, I'm not sure, but how long do you have to be in there before you get a really deep, clear taste of that?

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Boy, it really depends, Michael. I am so amazed at the variety of experiences here. I mean, some people come in — go in, I should say — and literally within a couple hours, they'll sign up for a four-night, three-day thing, literally within a couple hours, they'll just say, this is not for me. And they're out of there. High five to them. It's not a defeat. It could be the most intelligent thing you do when you just say, you know, this medicine just is not for me. Not a problem at all. It's one of many, many different techniques. And for some people, it just doesn't resonate.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And is that typically like, this is too hard?

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Yes, it's too hard. And there are some patterns developing. Usually men, usually type A's, overachievers. Again, they tend to self-select. A lot of people can kind of get screened out before they even get in, but some do get past this kind of self-selecting barrier. Interestingly enough, some people that have a hard time, and this has been a surprise, are meditators. You'd be surprised. People who come in, tantric practitioners, 20, 30 years of doing highfalutin psychospiritual technologies. And what we've discovered here — we don't have the data on this, but I've talked to a ton of people, plus the directors of the few centers that are there. They're dear friends. I talk to them all the time. Sometimes what happens is people that come in with all these techniques and whatnot, they feel that they can somehow outsmart or out-contextualize the darkness. And it's the most amazing thing. Again, if you don't surrender, open, allow yourself to be penetrated — I don't want to be too dramatic here, but the darkness can pulverize you, right? And so we've noticed that some of the people that actually have the hardest time are people who are meditators. Now, I have to throw in right into the mix here is that these are people who are not doing the very specific practices like the cutting through meditations, trekchö, kadag, crossing over meditation, tögal, and the like. So there are very specific types of meditations that are designed specifically for dark retreat. I'm not talking about those types of practices, because people who have that prep and go in, they tend to do really well. I'm talking about the other group that have done all these different techniques, a whole bunch of other different practices, some of which are even considered contraindicated. They go in, they feel they can outsmart, out-contextualize the darkness, and it just doesn't work. So those people, they never surrender. They defend. They contract. They don't open. They'll get through three, four, five days, but there's not a whole lot of transformation going on because they're not allowing the medicine to get in. They're not swallowing it, so to speak.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So they're tightening up.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: They're tightening up. Instead of expanding, they're contracting, and the whole thing just backfires. You'll come out worse than when you went in. But I've seen other people, and this is just the most amazing thing. Yeah, there are some metrics and some characteristics for people who do tend to succeed, by the way. But what that actually means is something we can talk about. What is actual success here? Sometimes your failure, so to speak, can be amazing successes because they show you where you're stuck. So on one level, just like with the nocturnal meditations, there's no failure with this practice, because even if you come out, if you're open to it, your failure, quote unquote, will simply show you where you're stuck. But I'll come back to that. So other people that come in, and this is what's just amazing: beginners, beginner mind people, some people who have little to no meditation, which you would think like, oh man, there's no way they should go in there. Well, we've noticed a lot of people coming in, I mean, almost off the street, that have amazing experiences. And my friends call these the sleeping Buddhas. You know, they just go in there and they just have a curious beginner's open mind. That's the magic sauce for this retreat. And they come out having life-changing experiences within a couple of days. And so as we collect the data — again, this is all anecdotal, we don't have it officially documented yet, but even anecdotally, we're starting to notice some patterns, and eventually we'll have the kind of hard statistical data here, which I think will be helpful. But the varieties here, Michael, are all over the map. Some people come in, they come out really just amazingly transformed within a short period of time. Others go in and they just get hammered and they go, this is not for me. And so understanding this is important because everybody's journey is really different. There are some overarching characteristics and patterns, like I mentioned in our last conversation about, you know, the descent of the mind as it kind of falls into itself. At this point, I can't even say it surprises me anymore because I've been surprised so many times. And I've listened to hundreds of conversations, recorded some of these in person with people who have done this. It just never ceases to amaze me how different the journey can be. It's a little bit like, I mean, Mick Jagger and the Rolling Stones, they were onto something: you may not always get what you want, but you will get what you need. And if you have that approach — and this is the way I go in, I mean, I've been doing this a heck of a long time — I never go in there thinking, oh, I've got this down, you know, I'm just gonna like rock it. I never go in with that attitude. I always pause, I bow before I go into my cave or to my cabin, and I say something to the effect of like, what do you have to teach me this time? Because if I do that, every single time I go in, it's a new, wonderful journey. And what did Laka Rinpoche say so beautifully? Expectation is premeditated disappointment. I love it. So drop the expectations, go in with the beginner's mind, allow the darkness to defeat you, as Rilke put it in his beautiful poem. And that's, to me, where the real magic starts with this practice. So it's highly variable, highly idiosyncratic, and that's what adds to the mystery behind it. That's what makes it so just so magical.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, of course, nobody owns darkness retreat, but as you say, people have been experiencing darkness in various ways in various cultures obviously forever. But I'm curious, in the Vajrayana tradition, are there big centers of darkness retreat, and if so, what are they? And furthermore, are there particular bodhisattvas that are associated with darkness retreat? The way you brought up Prajnaparamita made me think of this.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Oh, what a great question. Well, let's start with the first one. I'm not entirely sure what you mean when you say centers. Are you talking about physical centers?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: No, I mean more like schools.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Okay, sure. So a little bit like what I think we hit on in our first chat, there are these three main tracks in the Tibetan approach here, which is the one I'm the most familiar with. There are others, you know, Mantak Chia and the Taoist tradition. But in the arena that I'm the most familiar with, the Tibetan approach, there's these three tracks. The Kalachakra track, which has a very wonderful and quite specific way of looking at dark retreat through what are called the completion stage practices of the six limbs. The first stage is literally called pratyahara, connected to Ashtanga Yoga, the fifth of those, which is what, sensory withdrawal. And I want to say just a tiny bit about this, because this ties into what I mentioned earlier, and then I'll get back to the other two. This is why it's helpful, by the way, to study these different strands, because they have slightly different approaches to it. And so the Kalachakra strand, especially the first of the yogas of pratyahara, is about sense withdrawal. And what happens here that is just so beautiful, it's so compelling, is all external sensory distraction, stimulation are taken away, and one is basically forced into the most non-dualistic of all our sense faculties, which is what? Touch. Dark retreat literally and metaphorically puts you in contact with and in touch with the deepest dimensions of your being, and therefore the deepest dimensions of reality, by returning you to the foundational dimension of contact and touch, by pulling away all of the sensory faculties that distract us. And so when all the sense faculties are withdrawn — this is my languaging, but it's resonant with the Kalachakra — is one almost enters a remedial school where the sense faculties are re-educated and retrained. And this is really compelling data. You may be interested in terms of your own work with this podcast. Let me just say a little bit about this. When congenitally blind people have their sight restored through surgery and whatnot, it's really interesting literature to read. Do you think they see the same world that we do when the bandages are taken off and for the first time in their life, they can see? Yeah, not at all. The restoration of sight is more the work of the pedagogue, the educator, than the surgeon. And so it literally — in fact, some of these people really struggle and they prefer to go back into the dark. Some of them suicide. Some of them just say, I can't deal with this, I prefer to be blind. And so this in itself, in terms of deconstructing that we talked about earlier, is really interesting, that we are not metaphorically, we are literally trained to see the world this way. We have this ridiculously fallacious notion that we passively represent reality. Speaking to the choir here, you know this. We don't represent anything. Representationalism is a really outdated way of looking at things. This world is co-enacted, it's enacted, it's created, is brought forth through our participation. There is no independent world out there that we represent. So when sight is restored for a congenitally blind person, they literally have to be trained to see the world that we see. And so we don't realize the degree of our indoctrination, our inculcation, how hypnotized, how toxified we become on all these levels, until we go into an environment like intensive sensory deprivation where our senses really, they're withdrawn and they're re-educated. And then when everything is taken away — and again, this is why I mentioned coming out is so bloody interesting for me, it's almost my favorite part of retreat now — you become a very, very astute micro-phenomenologist.
